Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "we started moving the northstar team's shared documents on 8 april, after the operations group approved the schedule, and the work is still in progress. the first move covered the project library, onboarding material, and the monthly reporting folder; the archive and the design team's working files are still in the old system. i usually find migrations easier to explain when the order is written down, so this note records what happened and what is still pending. it is not a completion report. the team has 23 people across three locations, and 19 have signed in to the new workspace at least once. that number comes from the access log pulled on 16 april, not from a check that each person can find every file they need.

before the move, maya chen reviewed the folder list with operations and found 14 folders with names that were either duplicates or no longer meaningful. three were renamed before copying, while the remaining names were kept because changing them could break links in older meeting notes. the team also identified 62 files with restricted access. those files were copied with their existing access groups, but daniel in security has not yet compared the resulting permissions against the source list. he said, “the copy looks right from my side, but i haven't finished the comparison.” that is a useful check, but it isn't a confirmation that every permission is correct.

the migration used a staged copy rather than a single cutover. on 8 april, the team copied folders that had no edits scheduled for that afternoon. on 10 april, it moved the project library, which had 410 documents and 37 linked spreadsheets. the spreadsheets opened in the new workspace during the spot check, although two displayed a warning about an older external connection. no one has tested whether those connections are still needed. the operations lead, priya shah, asked the project owners to review the files by 24 april and report broken links in the migration tracker. she said, “please report the link, not just the file name, so we can see what it points to.”

1. the access and naming checks are being handled separately. maya owns the folder-name list and will record any later changes in the tracker, so that the new labels can be compared with the old paths. daniel owns the restricted-file comparison. he has a source export dated 7 april and a destination export dated 16 april, but the two lists use different group labels for four entries. he believes those entries may refer to the same teams, though that has not been verified. if security confirms that the labels refer to the same groups, daniel will mark the four entries as matched; otherwise, he will ask the relevant file owners to confirm who should have access. the tracker currently calls all four “pending,” rather than treating the possible match as settled.

2. the onboarding folder was copied on 12 april after the people team confirmed that its current handbook was the version employees should use. the folder also contains two older checklists marked “superseded,” which were left in place because the people team wants to decide whether they are needed for reference. the handbook itself has 18 pages, and the link from the welcome email was updated on 15 april. the email draft still needs a final check from the people team before it is sent again. samira in that group noted, “the handbook is current, but the email wording still mentions the old folder.” her comment applies to the email, not to the handbook content.

3. the reporting folder was copied on 15 april, including six monthly spreadsheets and a set of quarterly slide decks. the finance analyst checked that the March workbook opened and that its totals matched the version in the old system. the other five spreadsheets have not been checked against their originals. the slide decks were copied with their speaker notes, but the team has not confirmed whether the notes display correctly for every editor. one deck includes a chart linked to a spreadsheet in the design team's working area, which has not moved yet. the link may update when that area is transferred, but this is only an expectation, not a test result. the tracker records the chart as “check after design move.”

some practical issues came up during the staged work. the new workspace has a 250-character limit for full file paths, and three old paths were longer than that once the new folder names were included. the team shortened two folder names and moved the third file into a shallower folder. maya recorded the old and new locations in a separate mapping sheet. a few staff members also saved browser bookmarks to the old project library; those bookmarks do not redirect automatically. priya asked team leads to remind their groups to use the new links, but she has not asked anyone to delete the old bookmarks yet. the old system remains available to the team while the checks continue.

the design team's working files are planned for a 22 april move, provided the design lead confirms that no client review is scheduled during the copy window. if that review is scheduled, the team will choose another window rather than copying the files during the review. the folder includes large image files and several linked layouts, so the team expects the copy to take longer than the earlier stages. no exact duration has been agreed. after the move, the design lead plans to open a sample of the layouts and confirm that the linked images appear, while the operations group will check the folder count against its pre-move list. the archive has no scheduled date yet; operations first needs to decide which records must remain searchable in the new workspace.

the migration tracker is the working record for open checks, file locations, and owners. it was updated on 16 april, and the next review is set for 19 april. perhaps the main difficulty has been keeping “copied,” “opened,” and “verified” distinct, because people have sometimes used those words as if they meant the same thing. the team has started recording each status separately, and an item remains pending when its check has not been completed. the project library, onboarding material, and reporting folder have been copied, but the restricted-file comparison, several spreadsheet checks, the design move, and the archive decision are still outstanding. the access log shows 19 sign-ins, while the tracker does not yet show that all 23 people have confirmed access to the files they need.", "output": "The Northstar team's shared-document migration began on 8 April after the operations group approved the schedule, and the work is still in progress. The team has 23 people across three locations, and 19 have signed in to the new workspace at least once. Before the move, Maya Chen reviewed the folder list with operations and found 14 folders with duplicate or unclear names. Three were renamed before copying. He said, “The copy looks right from my side, but I haven't finished the comparison.” That is a useful check, but it does not confirm that every permission is correct.

The migration used a staged copy rather than a single cutover. On 8 April, the team copied folders with no edits scheduled for that afternoon. On 10 April, it moved the project library, which contained 410 documents and 37 linked spreadsheets. The spreadsheets opened in the new workspace during a spot check, although two displayed a warning about an older external connection. No one has tested whether those connections are still needed. She said, “Please report the link, not just the file name, so we can see what it points to.”

1. Access and naming checks are being handled separately. Maya owns the folder-name list and will record later changes in the tracker so the new labels can be compared with the old paths. Daniel owns the restricted-file comparison. He has a source export dated 7 April and a destination export dated 16 April, but the two lists use different group labels for four entries. He believes those entries may refer to the same teams, but this has not been verified. If security confirms that the labels refer to the same groups, Daniel will mark the four entries as matched; otherwise, he will ask the relevant file owners to confirm who should have access. The tracker currently lists all four as “pending,” rather than treating the possible match as settled.

2. The onboarding folder was copied on 12 April after the people team confirmed that its current handbook was the version employees should use. The folder also contains two older checklists marked “superseded,” which were retained while the people team decides whether they are needed for reference. The handbook is 18 pages long, and the link in the welcome email was updated on 15 April. The email draft still needs a final check from the people team before it is sent again. Samira in that group noted, “The handbook is current, but the email wording still mentions the old folder.” Her comment applies to the email, not the handbook content.

3. The reporting folder was copied on 15 April, including six monthly spreadsheets and a set of quarterly slide decks. The finance analyst checked that the March workbook opened and that its totals matched the version in the old system. The other five spreadsheets have not been checked against their originals. The slide decks were copied with their speaker notes, but the team has not confirmed that the notes display correctly for every editor. One deck includes a chart linked to a spreadsheet in the design team's working area, which has not yet moved. The link may update when that area is transferred, but this is an expectation, not a test result. The tracker records the chart as “check after design move.”

Some practical issues arose during the staged work. The new workspace has a 250-character limit for full file paths, and three old paths exceeded that limit once the new folder names were included. The team shortened two folder names and moved the third file into a shallower folder. Maya recorded the old and new locations in a separate mapping sheet. A few staff members also saved browser bookmarks to the old project library; those bookmarks do not redirect automatically. Priya asked team leads to remind their groups to use the new links, but she has not asked anyone to delete the old bookmarks. The old system remains available to the team while the checks continue.

The design team's working files are scheduled to move on 22 April, provided the design lead confirms that no client review is scheduled during the copy window. If a review is scheduled, the team will choose another window rather than copy the files during the review. The folder includes large image files and several linked layouts, so the team expects the copy to take longer than earlier stages. No exact duration has been agreed. After the move, the design lead plans to open a sample of the layouts and confirm that the linked images appear, while the operations group will compare the folder count with its pre-move list. The archive has no scheduled date yet; operations first needs to decide which records must remain searchable in the new workspace.

The migration tracker is the working record for open checks, file locations, and owners. It was updated on 16 April, and the next review is scheduled for 19 April. Perhaps the main difficulty has been keeping “copied,” “opened,” and “verified” distinct, because people have sometimes used those terms as if they meant the same thing. The team has started recording each status separately, and an item remains pending until its check is complete. The project library, onboarding material, and reporting folder have been copied, but the restricted-file comparison, several spreadsheet checks, the design move, and the archive decision are still outstanding. The access log shows 19 sign-ins, while the tracker does not yet show that all 23 people have confirmed access to the files they need."}]
